title: Pressure
summary: Learn about pressure in solids, liquids, and gases, Pascal's principle, and atmospheric pressure.
olay.h: Two hemispheres that horses could not pull apart
olay.p: Otto von Guericke joined two copper hemispheres and pumped out the air inside. Teams of horses hitched to each side could not pull them apart. What was holding them together?
cards.0.p: Pressure is the force acting perpendicular to a unit of surface, given by P = F / A. With force in newtons and area in m², the unit is the pascal. 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
cards.0.key: Pressure is a scalar and has no direction. The pressure force (F = P·A) is a vector.
cards.1.h: Pressure of solids: it is all about area
cards.1.p: The edge of a knife and the tip of a thumbtack create a large pressure with a small area. Snowshoes and tank tracks spread the weight over a wide area and reduce the pressure.
cards.1.key: For a uniform solid P = W/A = ρ·g·h. A solid transmits force, while an enclosed liquid transmits pressure.
cards.2.p: The pressure caused by the weight of a liquid is P = ρ·g·h (h is the depth, ρ the density). The shape of the container and the amount of liquid do not change it. Pressure is large at depth, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom.
cards.2.key: In water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) every 10 m of depth adds about 100 000 Pa.
cards.2.etk.soru: Change the depth and the liquid. Water 1000, olive oil ≈ 900, mercury 13 600 kg/m³. Liquid pressure only, g = 10 m/s².
cards.3.p: The force on the bottom is F = P·A, and it may not equal the weight of the liquid. In a straight container F = W. In a container that widens upward F < W, and in one that narrows F > W.
cards.3.svg#5: equal base areas: F = ρ·g·h·A is the same for all
cards.3.key: The force on a side wall comes from the average pressure: F = ρ·g·(h/2)·A.
cards.3.once.soru: Two containers with equal bases hold water to the same height. One widens upward and holds more water. Which one has the larger force on its bottom?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: F = P·A. The depth is the same, so the pressure is the same, and the base area is the same too. So the forces are equal. The sloping walls carry the weight of the extra water in the wide container.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The weight of the extra water rests on the sloping walls. The force on the bottom is P·A.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: The pressure and the base area are the same. So the force is the same too.
cards.4.p: Containers joined at the bottom are called connected vessels. When a single liquid is at rest, its surface is at the same level in every arm. Teapots and water towers work on this principle.
cards.4.svg#0: one liquid → same level in every arm
cards.4.key: If a U-tube holds two liquids that do not mix, then above their common level h₁·ρ₁ = h₂·ρ₂.
cards.4.once.soru: You pour water into a U-shaped tube. One arm is thin and the other is wide. Where do the surfaces settle when the water is at rest?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The pressure must be equal at points of the same depth. So the surfaces are on the same horizontal line. The width of the arm makes no difference.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The thin arm holds less water, but pressure depends only on depth.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: The wide arm holds more water, but pressure depends only on depth.
cards.5.p: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted unchanged to every point. This is Pascal's principle. In a hydraulic system F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂. So the force is multiplied by the same factor as the area.
cards.5.key: You gain in force but lose in distance. The large piston rises less, by the ratio of the areas.
cards.6.p: Air has weight too. Torricelli turned a tube full of mercury upside down, and at sea level the mercury stopped at 76 cm. That is why 1 atm = 76 cmHg ≈ 101 325 Pa.
cards.6.key: If you used water instead of mercury, the column would be about 10.3 m tall.
cards.6.once.soru: You put a card over a glass full of water and turn the glass upside down. The water does not spill. What holds the card?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Air has weight too. The pressure of the air on the card from below is much larger than the pressure of the water in the glass.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Adhesion alone cannot hold the card. The air pressure does the real work.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: A light card would fall by itself too. So something must be pushing it from below.
cards.7.p: As you go higher, atmospheric pressure drops, and water boils at a lower temperature. On Everest water boils at about 70 °C. A pressure cooker raises the pressure, and water boils above 100 °C.
cards.7.svg#0: sea level: 1 atm, water boils at 100 °C
cards.7.svg#6: P drops as you go up
cards.7.key: Boiling starts when the vapor pressure of the liquid (the pressure of its vapor) equals the outside pressure.
cards.8.p: Gas particles move all the time and hit the walls. These collisions create gas pressure, and the pressure is the same everywhere in the container. At constant volume, the pressure rises if the number of particles or the temperature increases.
cards.8.svg#0: gas: P is the same everywhere
cards.8.key: If the liquid in a manometer is lower by h on the gas side, the gas pressure is P₀ + ρ·g·h.
cards.8.once.soru: You heat a gas in a closed container. The volume does not change. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Heated particles speed up and hit the walls harder and more often. So the pressure increases.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The particles do not slow down, they speed up. So the collisions get stronger.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The number of particles is the same, but their speeds increased, so the collisions get stronger.
cards.9.p: The pressure at a point is the sum of all the pressures above it. In an open container P = P₀ + ρ·g·h. If there is gas above the liquid, you write the gas pressure in place of P₀.
cards.9.once.soru: You are 10 m deep in an open pool. The pressure of the air above is ≈ 100 000 Pa, and the pressure of 10 m of water is 100 000 Pa. What is the total pressure?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Pressures add up. The air gives 100 000 Pa and the water 100 000 Pa, for a total of 200 000 Pa, about 2 atm.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is only the pressure of the water. You must add the pressure of the air above the water too.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Pressures add up; you do not take their average.
cards.10.p: A fluid speeds up where its path narrows. By Bernoulli's principle, the pressure of a fluid drops where it speeds up. In a storm, fast wind over a roof lowers the pressure, and the air inside can push the roof off.
cards.10.svg#0: as speed goes up, pressure goes down
cards.10.key: When a fast train passes, stand behind the line on the platform. The fast air next to the train lowers the pressure.
cards.10.once.soru: You hold two sheets of paper face to face and blow between them. What do the sheets do?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The pressure of the air speeding up between the sheets drops. The pressure of the still air outside pushes the sheets inward.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Intuition says so, but the pressure of air drops when it speeds up.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The pressure drops in between, so the sheets move.
cards.11.p:
• Pressure is P = F / A, and its unit is the pascal.
• For a solid, a smaller area means a larger pressure.
• Liquid pressure is P = ρ·g·h, and it does not depend on the shape of the container.
• By Pascal's principle F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
• 1 atm = 76 cmHg ≈ 101 325 Pa, and it drops as you go higher.
quiz.0.q: In a hydraulic lift the small piston has an area of 10 cm² and the large one 200 cm². If you apply 50 N to the small piston, what is the largest load, in N, that the large piston can balance?
quiz.0.e: Since F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂, F₂ = 50 · 200 / 10 = 1000 N. The area is 20 times larger, so the force is 20 times larger too.
quiz.1.q: Put the liquid pressures at the given points in open containers in order from smallest to largest.
quiz.1.ogeler.2: 25 cm deep in salt water (ρ = 1.2 g/cm³)
quiz.1.e: P = ρ·g·h, and g is the same for all. So look at the products h·ρ: 20·1 = 20, 30·0.8 = 24, 25·1.2 = 30, and 10·13.6 = 136. Even at a small depth, mercury gives the largest pressure.
quiz.2.q: Three containers with equal base areas are filled with water to the same height. Match each container with the relation between the liquid force F on its bottom and the weight W of the water.
quiz.2.e: In all three F = ρ·g·h·A is the same. The widening container holds more water, so W is larger and F < W; the narrowing container holds less water, so F > W.
quiz.3.q: In an open-end manometer connected to a gas tank, the water in the open arm stands 30 cm higher than on the gas side. If atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa and g = 10 m/s², what is the pressure of the gas, in Pa?
quiz.3.e: If the water is higher in the open arm, the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure by ρ·g·h. So P = 100 000 + 1000·10·0.3 = 103 000 Pa.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Drop the brick, step on the snow, lower the diver, and lift the car.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Two bricks are identical, and each weighs 20 N. One stands upright and will touch the sponge with its small face. The other lies flat and will touch it with its wide face.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: When released, which one sinks deeper into the sponge?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The flat brick touches a wider area. Its weight is spread over a large area.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The force is the same, but the upright brick puts it on an area 4 times smaller. A smaller area means a larger pressure. The upright brick exerts 4000 Pa, and the flat one 1000 Pa.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The weights are equal, but the areas they touch are different.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: Do not sink into the snow
A:adimlar.1.metin: You weigh 600 N and you are standing on snow. This snow can hold a pressure of at most 3000 Pa. Make the area of your shoes larger and do not sink in.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 600 N ÷ 0.2 m² = 3000 Pa. Snowshoes do not change your weight. They spread it over a large area.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The density of water is 1000 kg/m³, and g is about 10 m/s². Lower the diver and watch the pressure. Stop at the depth where the water pressure is 200 000 Pa.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: 1000 × 10 × 20 = 200 000 Pa. When the depth doubled, the liquid pressure doubled too.
A:adimlar.3.metin: We will fill a wide, a narrow, and a funnel-shaped container with water to a height of 20 cm. The funnel holds the most water, and the narrow one the least.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: In which one is the liquid pressure at the bottom the largest?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The funnel holds the most water, but the formula is P = ρ·g·h, and the amount is not in it.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A wide base makes the total force larger, but the force on each unit of area stays the same.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Liquid pressure depends only on depth and density, and 1000 × 10 × 0.2 = 2000 Pa. The shape of the container and the amount of water make no difference. This is called the hydrostatic paradox.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The small piston has an area of 10 cm², and you apply 200 N to it. Find the smallest large piston that can hold up the 10 000 N car.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The large piston must have an area of 500 cm², 50 times the small one. 200 N × 50 = 10 000 N. But you lose in distance. If you push the small piston 50 cm, the car rises only 1 cm.
A:adimlar.5.metin: At sea level water boils at 100 °C. Go up and find the altitude where water boils at 80 °C.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: At about 6000 m the outside pressure drops so much that water boils at 80 °C. That is why food takes longer to cook on high mountains.
A:kapanis.0: Pressure is the size of the force acting perpendicular to a unit of surface, P = F / A. It is a scalar, and its unit is the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).
A:kapanis.1: For the same force, a smaller area means a larger pressure. That is why a knife cuts and why snowshoes keep you from sinking.
A:kapanis.2: Liquid pressure is P = ρ·g·h. It grows with depth and does not depend on the shape of the container or the amount of liquid.
A:kapanis.3: By Pascal's principle, pressure in an enclosed liquid is transmitted everywhere. In a hydraulic system F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
A:kapanis.4: Atmospheric pressure is 76 cmHg (1 atm) at sea level. It drops as you go higher, and water boils at a lower temperature.
